operations.original: [L3] Every integer is $n$ or $-n$ for a natural $n$, and every rational is $m/n$ with $m$ an integer and $n$ a natural $\ge 1$; the embeddings preserve sums and products, and $n \ne 0$ for $n \ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[def-integers]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).
operations.proposed:
[L3] The embeddings $\mathbb N\subseteq\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb R$ preserve arithmetic; the image of $\mathbb N$ in $\mathbb Z$ is exactly the nonnegative integers, and positive canonical naturals are nonzero ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]], [[lem-int-embeds-rat]], [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

[L5] Every rational is represented by a pair $(a,b)$ of integers with $b\ne0$, where $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ means $ad=cb$; rational multiplication and inversion are the pair operations ([[def-rationals]], [[def-rat-operations]]).

[L6] The integers form a totally ordered commutative ring ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]).

operations.original: 4.1 Claim 4: an integer $m$ is $n$ or $-n$ for some natural $n$. In the first case claim 3 applies directly. In the second, $f(mx) = f(-(nx)) = -f(nx) = -nf(x) = m f(x)$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3]
operations.proposed: 4.1 Claim 4: by the total order and addition compatibility in [L6], either $m\ge0$ or $-m\ge0$; by [L3] the nonnegative one is the image of some natural $n$. Thus $m=n$ or $m=-n$. In the first case claim 3 applies directly. In the second, $f(mx)=f(-(nx))=-f(nx)=-nf(x)=mf(x)$. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L3, L6]

operations.original: 5.1 Claim 5: let $q$ be rational and write $q = m/n$ with $m$ an integer and $n$ a natural $\ge 1$, so $n \ne 0$. Applying claim 4 with the integer $n$ to the real $qx$ gives $n f(qx) = f(n q x) = f(mx) = m f(x)$, and dividing by $n$ gives $f(qx) = (m/n) f(x) = q f(x)$. [step 4.1, L3, L4]
operations.proposed: 5.1 Claim 5: by [L5], write $q=[(a,b)]$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Z$ and $b\ne0$. By [L6], either $b>0$ or $-b>0$; in the second case replace $(a,b)$ by $(-a,-b)$, which represents the same rational because $a(-b)=(-a)b$. The resulting positive denominator is the image of a natural $n\ge1$ by [L3]; call the resulting numerator $m$. The pair formulas in [L5] give $[(m,n)]=[(m,1)]\,[(1,n)]=j(m)j(n)^{-1}$, where $j$ is the integer embedding, so after the field embedding into $\mathbb R$ this is $q=m/n$. By [L3], $n\ne0$. Applying claim 4 with the integer $n$ to the real $qx$ gives $nf(qx)=f(nqx)=f(mx)=mf(x)$, and division by $n$ gives $f(qx)=(m/n)f(x)=qf(x)$. [step 4.1, L3, L4, L5, L6, algebra]
